item.title: Schools to drive new era of Fiji rugby league
item.description: SCHOOLS will form the backbone of a new rugby league development program in Fiji, with Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) commissioner Peter Beattie revealing plans to introduce the sport to children from as young as five. item.content:encoded:
SCHOOLS will form the backbone of a new rugby league development program in Fiji, with Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) commissioner Peter Beattie revealing plans to introduce the sport to children from as young as five.

Beattie made the comments during an ARLC visit to Rishikul Nadera Primary School on Monday, as part of the newly established 10-year partnership with the Fiji National Rugby League.

He said the ARLC would work with the Education Department to develop a program that could be introduced in schools and provide children with opportunities to participate and develop through rugby league.

“We’ll be working with the Education Department, who we met yesterday (Monday), to come up with a program to be implemented in schools, obviously from an early age, even from five years old, all the way through, so that young people reach their full potential,” Beattie said.

The program will include a non-contact component, with a strong focus on encouraging both boys and girls to participate.

Beattie said the aim was not simply to identify future NRL players, but to use sport as a way of helping young Fijians lead healthier and more active lives.

“Some will have pathways where they go to become NRL players, both boys and girls, and some will never go to that level, which is fine,” he said.

“We just want young Fijians, as part of this program, to live a long, healthy life.”

Beattie said school competitions would also be developed, although the details would be worked out in consultation with the Education Department.

He stressed that rugby league would not be positioned as a rival to rugby union, saying young Fijians should be able to participate in both codes.

“We’re not in competition with the rugby union, they will have competitions, we will have competitions, players will play both rugby union and rugby league, and that’s fine,” he said.

item.title: Local prop earns chance
item.description: FOR years, Inoke Ravuiwasa has worked his way through Fiji’s domestic rugby ranks with one goal in mind — earning an opportunity at the highest level. The experienced tighthead prop has been signed by the Swire Shipping Fijian Drua for the 2027 Shop N Save Super Rugby Pacific season, rewarding a career built on perseverance, discipline and sacrifice.
item.content:encoded:
FOR years, Inoke Ravuiwasa has worked his way through Fiji’s domestic rugby ranks with one goal in mind — earning an opportunity at the highest level.

The experienced tighthead prop has been signed by the Swire Shipping Fijian Drua for the 2027 Shop N Save Super Rugby Pacific season, rewarding a career built on perseverance, discipline and sacrifice.

Originally from Tavuki, Taveuni, with maternal links to Susui, Vanuabalavu in Lau, Ravuiwasa has been a consistent performer in Fiji’s provincial competitions and a long-serving member of the Fiji Police rugby team.

He most recently represented Suva in the Skipper Cup after spending part of the 2026 season in Australia with the Western Districts Lions in Canberra’s John I Dent Cup.

His pathway to the Drua has also included representative rugby, having been part of the Fiji under-20 setup in 2016 alongside current Drua co-captains Temo Mayanavanua and Frank Lomani.

He later represented the Fijian Warriors against Australia Country in October last year and was also part of the Skipper Select side that faced the Drua in the club’s 2026 pre-season trial.

For Ravuiwasa, the signing is the reward for years of persistence.

“I’ve been working towards making this team for a long time, so to finally get this opportunity means a lot to me,” he said.

“All the sacrifices, perseverance and discipline over the years have paid off.”

The 30-year-old said the opportunity would only strengthen his determination to prove himself at Super Rugby Pacific level.

“I’m very grateful to the Drua management for giving me this opportunity, and I’ll continue to work hard, especially heading into the new season.”

Drua general manager Rugby Baden Stephenson said Ravuiwasa’s persistence had earned him his chance.

“He is an experienced and powerful tighthead prop who has consistently performed in Fiji’s domestic competitions, and his hard work and persistence over the years have earned him this opportunity,” Stephenson said.

item.title: Coach eyes talent
item.description: THE Crest Fiji Secondary Schools Netball Championships got underway in Suva yesterday, providing an established pathway for identifying and developing players who could progress to the Fiji Pearls. For new Pearls head coach Michelle Parsons, the tournament is an important part of that pathway as she looks to build a stronger connection between secondary schools netball and the national high-perfor
item.content:encoded:
THE Crest Fiji Secondary Schools Netball Championships got underway in Suva yesterday, providing an established pathway for identifying and developing players who could progress to the Fiji Pearls.

For new Pearls head coach Michelle Parsons, the tournament is an important part of that pathway as she looks to build a stronger connection between secondary schools netball and the national high-performance program.

Parsons watched the opening day at the Jay Narayan College grounds at Rewa St, Suva, and was encouraged by the level of talent on display.

“This is a really important pathway for netball,” Parsons said.

“We’re looking to introduce national development camps right across the country so we can develop girls in their regions, and then hopefully bring together a national team.”

The planned regional camps would complement the existing school pathway by giving talented players opportunities to continue their development in their respective regions before progressing into the national program.

Parsons said youth development would form part of the Pearls’ high-performance program, placing greater emphasis on identifying players early and giving them a clear route towards the national team.

Her assessment of the opening day was encouraging.

She was impressed by the girls’ ball skills, their ability to take strong catches, maintain their balance and create opportunities for long-range shots.

But Parsons is looking for more than technical ability.

The national coach wants young players to develop the confidence to make decisions, express themselves and play with freedom.

“What I’m really excited about looking at though is how people play.

“We don’t want them to be programmed, we want them to play with some freedom and really enjoy the game that they’re playing.”

Parsons believes the competition will provide a valuable gauge of the players’ development as it progresses, with the later stages expected to reveal more about their composure and consistency under pressure.

And with her plans for youth development extending beyond the championship, Parsons wants the girls to understand the opportunity in front of them.

“Think big and be courageous,” she said.

“This is the place where it’s okay to make mistakes and learn from them, but this is where you fall in love with the game.”

For the players, the championship remains a fight for school honours.

For Parsons, it is also an important part of the established journey from secondary schools netball towards the Fiji Pearls.

item.title: Pillay takes top honours at Ba Open
item.description: SHAKEEL Pillay produced an outstanding performance to claim the overall gross title at the 56th R.C. Manubhai Ba Open Golf Tournament, which concluded at the FSC Ba Golf Club last Sunday. The two-day tournament brought together golfers from across the country, with players showcasing skill, determination and sportsmanship.
item.content:encoded:
SHAKEEL Pillay produced an outstanding performance to claim the overall gross title at the 56th R.C. Manubhai Ba Open Golf Tournament, which concluded at the FSC Ba Golf Club last Sunday.

The two-day tournament brought together golfers from across the country, with players showcasing skill, determination and sportsmanship.

R.C. Manubhai Group of Companies director Rajesh Patel said the company was proud to continue its long-standing support of the Ba Open, which provides an important platform for golfers to showcase their talent.

Pillay was among the top performers by Ravendra Lal, who finished runner-up in the overall gross category.

Mohd Ali won the overall nett title, while Damon Chen finished runner-up.

In the women’s division, Raina Kumar claimed the overall gross title while Lynn Natividad took overall nett honours.

In the professional category, Roneel Prakash finished first, with Tomasi Tuivuna placed second.

The tournament highlighted the depth of golfing talent and provided an opportunity for players to strengthen ties within the wider golfing community.

R.C. Manubhai congratulated all winners and participants and acknowledged the organising committee, officials, supporters and others involved in delivering another successful Ba Open.

The company said its continued sponsorship reflects its commitment to supporting local sport, recognising talent and creating opportunities for communities.

As a long-standing supporter, R.C. Manubhai said it looks forward to continuing its association with the Ba Open next year.

item.title: National hockey crown wide open after gripping start
item.description: THE battle for Fiji’s secondary schools hockey crowns is already shaping into a fiercely contested affair after defending champions were pushed to their limits on the opening day of the Fiji Secondary Schools National Hockey Tournament in Lautoka yesterday. With the country’s top young hockey players gathered at the Nadovu Grounds, the national tournament wasted little time producing drama, upsets
item.content:encoded:
THE battle for Fiji’s secondary schools hockey crowns is already shaping into a fiercely contested affair after defending champions were pushed to their limits on the opening day of the Fiji Secondary Schools National Hockey Tournament in Lautoka yesterday.

With the country’s top young hockey players gathered at the Nadovu Grounds, the national tournament wasted little time producing drama, upsets and tight finishes across the under-16 and under-19 boys and girls divisions.

Defending under-16 boys champions Marist Brothers High School (MBHS) were given an early wake-up call, fighting out a 2-2 draw with Tilak High School (THS).

There was more evidence that no team would have an easy path to the national title when debutants Kalabu Secondary School (KSS) announced their arrival.

The newcomers held Suva Grammar School (SGS) to a 1-1 draw in the U16 boys grade, while their U16 girls showed plenty of determination in a narrow 1-0 defeat to THS.

Saint Thomas High School (STHS) emerged with an important win in the under-19 girls competition, edging Adi Cakobau School (ACS) 2-1.

Defending U19 girls champions SGS opened with a 2-0 victory over THS before being held to a scoreless draw by Suva Jai Narayan College (SJSS), another result underlining the unpredictable nature of the competition.

The U19 boys competition also delivered an early setback for defending champions Levuka Public School (LPS), who went down 1-0 to THS.

MBHS began their campaign with a 1-0 win over Suva Christian School (SCHS), while Dudley High School (DMHS) edged SGS by the same scoreline.

In the U16 girls competition, ACS made a statement with a 3-0 win over SGS, while Suva Jai Narayan College (SJC) swept aside KSS 5-0.

John Wesley High School (JWHS) and ACS played out a 1-1 draw, while SJSS and SGS could not be separated in their U19 girls clash, finishing scoreless.

Thirteen schools, including tournament newcomers KSS, are represented at the national championship, with 38 teams from Suva, Lautoka and Ovalau competing for four national titles.

After an opening day in which champions were challenged and newcomers showed they belonged, the race to be crowned Fiji’s best school hockey teams is wide open.

item.title: Tuvu’s historic double run
item.description: TUVU Primary School has given its school community plenty to celebrate after producing a historic campaign at the recent Lautoka Primary Inter- Primary Football Competition. For the first time in the school’s history, both the boys’ and girls’ teams reached the finals, finishing the tournament as proud runners-up.
item.content:encoded:
TUVU Primary School has given its school community plenty to celebrate after producing a historic campaign at the recent Lautoka Primary Inter- Primary Football Competition.

For the first time in the school’s history, both the boys’ and girls’ teams reached the finals, finishing the tournament as proud runners-up.

For head coach Avnil Naidu, the achievement was about more than the trophies. It was a reflection of the commitment, discipline and determination shown by the young players throughout the tournament.

The boys enjoyed a memorable run to the final, recording a nil-all draw against Warabetia Muslim, a 2-0 victory over Dreketi Sangam, another nil-all draw against Satya Sai and a 1-0 win over Qalito.

Their reward was a place in the final against Warabetia Muslim, where they fought bravely before going down 1-0 in a closely contested encounter.

For the girls, reaching the final continued a remarkable run of consistency. Tuvu has now recorded three consecutive runners-up finishes in the girls’ competition — a feat that highlights the strength and development of the school’s football program.

The girls defeated Satya Sai 1-0 and Qalito 1-0, while suffering a 2-0 loss to Dreketi Sangam and drawing nil-all with Warabetia Muslim in the earlier matches.

They earned another opportunity to claim the title when they faced Dreketi Sangam in the final, but after a tense contest, the match was decided on penalties.

Although both teams fell just short of the ultimate prize, their performances have created a significant milestone for Tuvu Primary.

Naidu praised his players for their courage, discipline and teamwork, while also acknowledging the families and supporters who stood behind the teams throughout the competition.

The strong support from the sidelines, he said, gave the players the energy to keep fighting.

The campaign was also a reflection of the work put in behind the scenes, with Naidu guiding the teams and Shanita Naidu managing the teams with care a partnership that has helped create a positive football environment for the young players.

For Tuvu Primary, the Inter-Primary campaign is more than a collection of results. It represents progress. It represents belief and most importantly, it has shown the school’s young footballers that they can compete with the best in Lautoka.

With both teams reaching the finals and the girls maintaining their remarkable three-year run as runners-up, Tuvu Primary has laid a strong foundation for an even brighter future in school football.

item.title: Leone’s homecoming
item.description: AT 38, Leone Nakarawa is at an age when most rugby players are thinking about life after the game. The Swire Shipping Fijian Drua, however, believe he still has plenty to give.
item.content:encoded:
AT 38, Leone Nakarawa is at an age when most rugby players are thinking about life after the game.

The Swire Shipping Fijian Drua, however, believe he still has plenty to give.

The return of one of Fiji’s most decorated forwards for the 2027 Shop N Save Super Rugby Pacific season is more than a homecoming.

It is a calculated gamble on experience, leadership and a player who has spent much of his career proving doubters wrong.

Nakarawa has been around the rugby world. He has played 132 professional matches for Glasgow Warriors, Racing 92, Toulon and Castres, earned 68 Flying Fijians caps, won an Olympic gold medal in Rio and lifted the PRO12 title with Glasgow.

He was named Player of the Match in Glasgow’s 2015 final victory over Munster, selected in the official Team of the Tournament at the 2015 Rugby World Cup and crowned the 2018 EPCR European Player of the Year. That is a career most players can only dream of. But the question now is simple.

What does a 38-year-old Nakarawa have left in the tank? Drua head coach Brad Mooar has no doubts.

“This is a big signing for the Drua. He will have a huge impact on and off the field for us every day,” Mooar said.

“His on field ability and experience is exceptional and suits exactly how we want to play.”

Those words are significant. The Drua are not bringing Nakarawa back simply to provide a famous name in the dressing room. They believe his playing style fits the way they want to play.

And then there is the part Mooar believes could be even more important.

“Having Leone’s leadership, his knowledge of the game and of the life and habits of a professional sportsman will be a huge benefit for our players to get side by side with Leone and learn from him every day,” Mooar said.

That could be Nakarawa’s greatest contribution.

The Drua have a young squad that needs players who understand what it takes to survive the pressure of Super Rugby Pacific. Nakarawa has been there.

He has played in Rugby World Cups, European finals, championship matches and an Olympic final. He knows the difference between playing rugby and performing when everything is on the line.

And Fiji has already seen what can happen when the Drua back experience.

Last season, Vereimi Vakatawa arrived amid questions over his age and whether his best rugby was behind him.

Critics questioned whether the former France international was nearing the end of his career. Instead, Vakatawa produced a breakthrough season and showed that an experienced player can still make a major impact.

Nakarawa now could provide another answer to the age debate. The offload maestro has never needed to rely solely on youth.

His game has always been built around instinct, intelligence, timing and an ability to see opportunities other players do not. Those qualities do not disappear simply because the birth certificate gets older.

For Nakarawa, though, this is about more than rugby. Raised in Matanagata, Vatukoula, the Kadavu native travelled from Fiji’s domestic rugby system and the Republic of Fiji Military Forces to the Fiji Warriors, the Flying Fijians and eventually the biggest stages in world rugby.

Mooar said the Drua were “thrilled” to welcome Nakarawa and his family into the Drua Vuvale/Vuniwere.

True to his reputation as a man of few words, Nakarawa needed only a few words to explain what the opportunity means.

“Looking forward to be playing for the Drua and playing professional and staying in Fiji.”

For Fiji’s rugby public, the fascination will be whether the veteran can turn experience into impact. At 38, nobody expects the Nakarawa of 2015 to walk back onto the field.

The Drua are hoping for something different. They want the Nakarawa of 2027 — wiser, battle-hardened and still capable of producing the moments that made him one of Fiji’s most feared forwards.

If Vakatawa showed last season that age can be deceptive, Nakarawa now has the chance to prove it all over again.

And this time, he will be doing it at home.
